messages.subject: truncated poisson?
parts:

Does the truncation operation T work for distributions other than normal? I have tried the following code, but STAN generated errors "no matches for function name="poisson_cdf""

################
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> Y[N]; 
}

}
transformed parameters {

}

    }

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] truncated poisson?
parts:
It only works for distributions that have
a _cdf version. You can look in the manual
index to quickly see which ones this is.

We're going to be writing more of these as
we go. For now, it'd be a bit tricky to do it
by hand in Stan because you need the incomplete
gamma function:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_gamma_function

Its recursive definition (given above) could be coded
iteratively in Stan itself, but it's not trivial.

If you're interested, I can provide some more help
on how to do that. Or we could prioritize
its addition to Stan. Along with the log-parameterizerd
Poisson, so instead of poisson(exp(alpha)), we could
write poisson_log(alpha). exp() is a dangerous floating-point
operation due to the risk of underflow and overflow.

- Bob

I don't know these models. Did you mean zero-inflated?
Or truncating below at 1 (inclusive)? Truncating below
at 0 (inclusive) won't do anything since that's the limit
of their support.

> Also right-truncated models are also useful. These can be done in JAGS. Poisson and
> Neg-bin are so widely used. I hope you could implement the log-parameterizerd Poisson and Neg-bin and add T[] to these
> two distributions.

We'll probably have the basic and log scale versions by the
end of the year or early in January. We'll announce them when
they're out on this list.

> Also I would like to report some typos in the manuscript and give some suggestions :
>
> (1) Page 5: Then make the library with the folloiwng make command.
> (2) Page 132: real bernoulli_logit_log(ints y, reals theta) <-- Should "theta" be "alpha"?
> (3) Page 115: for if_else in 20.3. Logical Functions, could you give some examples of "cond" because I could not found
> any logical operators, such as "==", "&＆". It seems that the function equals() has not implemented yet.

Our intention is also to add the full set of comparison
operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) and boolean operators
(&&, ||, !) as well as if-else and while constructs. It's
been tough prioritizing what to do! Luckily, we designed the
entire code base to be extensible, so we hope to hit almost
everything on our current to-do list over the next year or two.
We'll get to conditionals sooner than that, though, as it
won't be too hard of an addition.

Here's what I added to the doc:

Currently, Stan's logical abilities are very limited. Like C++, BUGS,
and R, Stan uses 0 to encode false, and 1 to encode true. The only
conditional-like operator is \Verb|if_else()| and the only logical
output operator is \Verb|step()|.

Until Stan gets comparison and boolean operations, these must be
hacked with various flavors of arithmetic. To test if a variable
\code{x} is greater than or equal to \code{y}, use \code{step(x - y)}.
To test if \code{x} equals \code{y}, use \code{step(x-y) * step(y-x)};
to test for zero, use \code{step(x) * step(-x)}.

For conjunction, use multiplication; for disjunction, use use addition
of absolute values. Negation is the same as testing for zero.

I'll elminate this text when the conditional and comparison operators
are in.

I've also thanked you in the acknowledgements (and looked up earlier
doc commentors and thanked them, too). I would've missed any
mailing-list-only corrections.

There's also the Marcus hack for conditionals, coding "if (cond) statement"
where cond is 0 or 1, use "for (i in 1:cond) statement". I can't
bring to put that suggestion in the manual. I must get conditionals
in the language before I have to document that hack in the manual, too.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] truncated poisson?
parts:
On 11/19/12 7:24 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, November 19, 2012 2:07:15 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> We're going to be writing more of these as
> we go. For now, it'd be a bit tricky to do it
> by hand in Stan because you need the incomplete
> gamma function:
>

> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution>
>
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_gamma_function <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_gamma_function>

>
> Its recursive definition (given above) could be coded
> iteratively in Stan itself, but it's not trivial.
>
>
> Wouldn't it be easier for Stan to use the CDF parameterization whose R code is
>
> exp(-lambda) * sum(lambda^(0:y) / factorial(0:y))

> You could easily do log1m(that) in a .stan file to integrate out the truncated mass.

That will overflow for large y. But we can compute stably on the
log scale, which is what we need anyway:

log poisson_cdf(y|lamba)

= -lambda + log SUM_{n=0}^y pow(lambda,n) / gamma(n+1)

= -lambda + LOG_SUM_EXP_{n=0}^y log[pow(lambda,n) / gamma(n+1)]

= -lambda + LOG_SUM_EXP_{n=0}^y [n * log(lambda) - lgamma(n+1)]

This should work for very modestly sized y. But with y values
of any size, the loops will be slow and consume a lot of space on
the auto-dif stack.

I sure hope there's an efficient incomplete gamma on the
log scale the way there's an efficient log gamma function.
Michael's been looking into not only the CDFs, but their
gradients.

- Bob

parts: Unfortunately I haven't been able to find one. There are some theoretical difficulties (the incomplete functions don't have the same symmetries/recurrence relations as their complete counterparts) but there should be enough structure to be able to expand the power series definitions through the log to build something mildly efficient. But that is far outside of my experience, and I'm guessing there hasn't been enough need to make it worthwhile for the experts.

Hurdle count models are two-component models with a truncated (at zero) count component (y = 1, 2, 3, ....) for positive counts and a hurdle component that models the zero counts. See http://rss.acs.unt.edu/Rdoc/library/pscl/html/hurdle.html.

(1) Page 132: in the Bernoulli pmf, c and y are mixed
(2) Poisson distribution (bottom line of Page 134): lambda! should be ”n!“.
(3) Page 133: for Categorical Distribution, y and n are mixed.

parts:
Here is a worked example of a right truncated Poisson model by calculating the truncated pmf directly using lp__. In the following code, I ran the stan model for some truncated Poisson data (Poisson(lambda = 5)T[，Cutpoint = 5]), i.e., y = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

The posterior mean of lambda = 5.006 is very close to the true value. I also used the gamlss package to fit the model. It estimated lambda as 5.129.

require(glamlss)
require(glamlss.tr)
(model_Pois <- gamlss(Y~1, data = data_tr, family= trun(Cutpoint+1, "PO", "right")))
exp(1.635) 
[1] 5.129458


# stan results:
> print(fit_pois_trunc, digits=3)

            mean se_mean    sd      2.5%       25%       50%       75%     97.5% n_eff  Rhat
lambda     5.006   0.003 0.131     4.754     4.912     5.003     5.097     5.263  2184 1.001

#~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
# Generate some fake truncated Poisson data
#~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

# true Poisson mean
lambda = 5
rp = rpois(1000, lambda)

Cutpoint = 5

# censoring
#rp_cens = rp
#rp_cens[rp_cens>Cutpoint] = Cutpoint

# truncation
rp_tr = subset(rp, rp <= Cutpoint)

# use gamlss
require(gamlss.tr)

# truncated Poisson random var. generating function
Pois_tr <- trun.r(par=c(Cutpoint), family="PO", type="right")

rp_tr = Pois_tr(1000, mu = lambda)
mean(rp_tr)
var(rp_tr)

barplot(table(rp_tr))

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
barplot(table(rp), main="Full data", xlim=c(0, 15))
barplot(table(rp_tr), main="trunc", xlim=c(0, 15))

# data for stan
data_tr = list(N = length(rp_tr), Cutpoint = Cutpoint, Y = rp_tr)

#~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
# stan model for the truncated Poisson data
#~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

model_trunc_poiss <- "

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> Y[N];
int<lower=0> Cutpoint;

}
parameters {
  real  c0;
}
transformed parameters {
  real lambda;
  lambda <- exp(c0);
}
model {
real cum_prob;

c0 ~ normal(0, 1000);
    for (i in 1:N)
    {

// truncated Poisson: not work yet for stan up to v1.0.3-2
      //Y[i] ~ poisson(lambda) T[0,C];
      
      // hand coded version
      cum_prob <- 0;
      for (k in 1:Cutpoint)
        cum_prob <- cum_prob + exp(poisson_log(k, lambda));

      lp__ <- lp__ + poisson_log(Y[i], lambda)-log(cum_prob);
    }
}
"

require(rstan)

inits = list(list(c0 = log(lambda+2)), list(c0 = log(1)))

fit_pois_trunc <- stan(model_code = model_trunc_poiss, data = data_tr, init = inits, iter = 5000, chains = 2)

print(fit_pois_trunc, digits=3)
traceplot(fit_pois_trunc, inc_warmup = FALSE)
